subject: Agriculture
title: Credit and Rural Banks
description: A fast breakdown of Credit and Rural Banks for builders.

hook.text: Seeds, fertilizer, and irrigation cost money. Poor farmers needed loans—but banks ignored rural areas.

buildup.text: India nationalized banks in 1969 partly to force lending to rural areas for Green Revolution inputs.

discovery.text: Access to credit let small farmers buy improved seeds and fertilizer. Adoption accelerated rapidly.

twist.text: Debt became a trap. One bad harvest and farmers couldn't repay loans—leading to cycles of poverty.

climax.text: India's ongoing farm debt crisis—and tragic farmer suicides—traces partly to Green Revolution-era credit policies.

punchline.text: Credit opened the door to progress—and to debt.

quiz.question: Why did India nationalize banks in 1969?
options: Partly to force rural lending for Green Revolution inputs

details.summary: The Green Revolution's input-intensive technology required farmers to purchase seeds, fertilizer, and irrigation equipment—costs that demanded access to credit. This topic covers how rural banking systems expanded to finance agricultural modernization and why credit access became a driver of.
details.whyItMatters: Access to credit determined which farmers could adopt Green Revolution technology. In many countries, wealthier farmers with land collateral got loans while smallholders could not, widening the rural wealth gap even as national food production.
takeaways: Green Revolution technology required upfront cash for seeds, fertilizer, and irrigation
Rural banking expanded dramatically in India and Southeast Asia to finance adoption
Credit access became a key divider between farmers who benefited and those left behind

faq.question: Why was credit so important for Green Revolution adoption?
faq.answer: Traditional farming used saved seeds and natural fertility at minimal cash cost. Green Revolution farming required purchasing improved seeds, synthetic fertilizer, and often irrigation equipment every season.

faq.question: How did credit access create inequality during the Green Revolution?
faq.answer: Banks required land as collateral for agricultural loans. Larger landowners obtained credit easily and adopted new technology first, increasing their profits and buying more land. Landless laborers and small tenants could not access loans, fell further behind, and many were displaced from farming.
